problems.description: Base64-encodes every message on top of a WebSocket text frame; the wire protocol already handles UTF-8 framing, so this adds ~33% payload bloat plus encode/decode code paths and a second place for serialization bugs to hide, with no compensating benefit.

NotificationServer.broadcast catches a bare Exception and silently evicts the client, conflating transient send errors (or even encoding failures) with disconnects and masking real faults in the registry.

13 convention violations (measured, convention score 0.78): module-level constants in broker.py/store.py should be UPPER_CASE, and test classes in test_app.py/test_channels.py/test_history.py should use PascalCase — diverging from the seed's own UPPER_CASE constant style (DATABASE).

The seed Flask Todo API was deleted wholesale and replaced with a different framework (websockets) rather than adapting existing seams; defensible for a greenfield session but it discards all prior structure and is why respects_existing_patterns is false.

strengths: Modular decomposition into ClientRegistry, NotificationServer, broker.py and store.py — clear separation of connection lifecycle, routing, and persistence.
Thread-safe ClientRegistry with a single lock, idempotent remove(), and snapshot() returning a consistent copy for iteration.
Tests added across test_app.py, test_channels.py, test_history.py covering the three message types and history persistence.
No new bugs and no duplication introduced (SonarQube: bugs +0, duplications +0.0%).
commit_reviews.summary: Session 1 delivers a cleanly modular WebSocket notification server, but ships an unnecessary base64 wire-encoding layer, a silent exception-swallowing broadcast, and 13 convention violations that diverge from the seed's UPPER_CASE constants and PascalCase classes.

problems.description: message_channel() reads the channel from two locations (top-level 'channel' or inside payload), creating a dual-source contract that can diverge and makes routing behavior harder to reason about.
Channel-cleanup logic (discard member, drop empty channel) is duplicated between remove() and unsubscribe() — consistent with the +8.7% duplication delta.

New test_channels.py introduces naming violations (Classes should use PascalCase, module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE), contributing to the 0.78 convention score; remaining listed violations are in broker.py/store.py/test_app.py/test_history.py and pre-date this diff.
broadcast_to_channel() calls registry.get() per subscriber under a lock and encodes once for all — acceptable at current scale, O(n) serialized sends are the dominant cost.

strengths: Extends the existing lock-protected ClientRegistry with _subscriptions/_channels maps, preserving the established thread-safety pattern
New REST endpoints reuse the existing process_request/Response idiom and hoist the JSON header construction out of the /health branch
subscribe/unsubscribe and broadcast-to-channel reuse the same send-failure -> registry.remove exception idiom as the existing broadcast path
Zero new bugs and one fewer smell per SonarQube, with a new test file covering channel routing
commit_reviews.summary: A cleanly fitted additive feature that extends the existing registry/dispatch/REST patterns with no new bugs and fewer smells, at the cost of minor duplication, a dual-source channel-extraction ambiguity, and a few naming violations in the new test file.

problems.description: Asymmetric lifecycle event flow: the 'connected' system message is sent only to the new client and never published to the broker, while 'disconnected' is broadcast only to local connections — both bypass the broker channel that all application messages now route through.

Direct messages targeting a client not in the local registry are silently dropped in deliver(); correct cross-node behavior depends entirely on broker-side routing keyed off set_client_state, which this diff does not exercise or verify.

_broker_task is stored on the instance but never awaited or cancelled in close(); the listener task's lifecycle is delegated implicitly to broker.close() with no explicit teardown of the stored handle.
store.save() persists every inbound message including subscribe/unsubscribe control traffic, potentially polluting message history with non-content events.

Convention score 0.78 with 13 violations: module-level constants in new broker.py and store.py are not UPPER_CASE, and test classes across test_app/test_channels/test_history use non-PascalCase naming (per static analysis).
A single integration session adds +526/-29 lines, 12 functions and 4 classes while raising cognitive complexity by +42 with 3 new smells — the deliver()/dispatch() routing branches grew considerably.

strengths: Message flow is cleanly centralized: dispatch now persists then publishes, and the server's broker subscription is the single delivery path — no re-broadcast loop despite the server publishing to the same channel it subscribes to.
Client connection/subscription state is mirrored to the broker on connect, subscribe/unsubscribe, and disconnect — a coherent foundation for a multi-node pub/sub design.
Defensive query-string parsing (manual split + parse_qs + guarded int casts) and a paginated /messages endpoint are added cleanly.
New tests added across three modules (app, channels, history) and code duplication reduced -4.1%.
Existing patterns preserved: make_message, message_channel, and the broadcast/dispatch structure carry forward unchanged.
commit_reviews.summary: Session 3's broker+store integration is a sound architectural direction that centralizes message flow with added tests and reduced duplication, but it lands with real technical debt — cognitive complexity +42, 3 smells, 13 convention violations (score 0.78) — plus a few lifecycle edge cases (task teardown, asymmetric system-event routing, silent direct-message drops) that keep the verdict neutral.

problems.description: BaseTransport.receive is declared as an abstract async generator, so its `raise NotImplementedError` body only fires on first iteration, not at call/instantiation time — abstract async-generator enforcement is awkward and a subclass could silently defer the failure.
process_request still depends on websockets.http11.Response and the REST/upgrade path remains WebSocket-coupled; the transport abstraction does not yet cover the connection-accept/HTTP layer.

on_connect is invoked before the client is registered (registry.add happens after), and it is a no-op in WebSocketTransport — a transport cannot reference the newly connected client inside on_connect.

Measured convention violations (module-level constants not UPPER_CASE in broker.py/store.py; non-PascalCase classes and constants in test files) all sit in files outside this diff — pre-existing repo debt, not introduced by the commit.

strengths: Clean extraction of a pluggable transport layer (BaseTransport ABC + WebSocketTransport), decoupling the core server from wire-format details while it retains routing, subscriptions, and persistence.

Dependency injection via `transport or make_transport(self.registry)` mirrors the existing make_broker factory pattern and respects the repo's conventions (PascalCase classes, snake_case functions, type hints, dataclass-style docstrings).
Zero new bugs or smells (SonarQube delta +0/+0) and reduced duplication (-0.4%); encode/decode consolidated into transport.py.
Broadcast error handling and registry cleanup remain centralized, and the change is additive — new transport implementations can be selected via the TRANSPORT env var.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, low-risk transport-abstraction refactor that decouples the notification server from WebSocket specifics with proper DI and no new defects; the 0.78 convention score reflects pre-existing violations in untouched files (broker.py, store.py, tests) rather than anything this commit introduces.
